title: Lalibela
hookLine: in Ethiopia, churches carved downward out of solid rock

cards: On a plain of reddish stone in the Ethiopian highlands, at first there's nothing to see. Then the ground opens.
At the bottom of a deep trench, its roof level with the plain, stands a church: doors, windows and a cross on top, all one piece with the rock around it. Nobody built it up. Somebody dug it down.
Pilgrims in white shawls climb down stone steps into the trenches to pray.

teach.b: Lalibela is a town in northern Ethiopia, named for a king the Ethiopian Orthodox Church honors as a saint.

Tradition says King Lalibela wanted a holy city in his own land, a new Jerusalem, for Christians who couldn't make the long journey to the old one. And so, the tradition goes, churches were cut out of the living rock.
The carvers started from the top.

teach.h: CUT FROM THE TOP, HOLLOWED FROM INSIDE.
teach.b: They cut a trench around a huge block of stone, leaving it standing free, then hollowed it from inside: rooms, pillars, arches, windows, nothing added. Cut away too much, and there was no putting it back.
One church is shaped like a cross when seen from above, its roof flat with the ground.
The place carries names from the Holy Land; a stream there is called the Jordan. Ethiopian Christianity has its own way.
Its church belongs to the family of Oriental Orthodox churches, with its own language of worship, Ge'ez, its own calendar and its own feasts.

teach.h: NOT ON THE ROCK. IT IS THE ROCK.
teach.b: At Christmas, which Ethiopian Christians call Genna, crowds of pilgrims fill the trenches and the rock-cut courtyards. Isaiah has a line that fits, in the King James Bible: "look unto the rock whence ye are hewn."
And Jesus, in Matthew, says, "upon this rock I will build my church." At Lalibela, that image becomes stone you can touch. The church isn't set on the rock.

how: Ethiopian Orthodox Christians make pilgrimage to Lalibela, especially at Genna, their Christmas, and at Timkat, the feast of Jesus's baptism, gathering in white shawls in the rock-cut churches to pray and sing.

games.why: they started from the top, freed a block with a trench, then carved rooms, pillars and windows inside. nothing was added, so nothing could be undone.

practice: The carvers at Lalibela made room by taking away. Look at the week ahead and find one hour you could cut free, the way they cut a trench around a block of stone: early in the morning, a lunch break, an evening without a screen.
If you pray, that hour can be for prayer; if you don't, let it be for quiet, a walk, or a long look at something beautiful.

wordCard.voice: Lalibela. A town in Ethiopia, named for a saint-king, where churches were carved down into solid rock as a new Jerusalem.
